posts.text:
AI is making it easier to do more marketing.

But what if we're getting better at producing work, not better at marketing?
More content.
More campaign ideas.
More headlines.
More experiments.

And on paper, that looks like productivity.

But there's a question I keep coming back to:
Are we creating more because it adds value, or simply because we can?

A content calendar can be full and still lack direction.

A campaign can have dozens of creative variations and still miss the audience.

A team can ship more assets without getting any closer to understanding what its customers actually care about.

I think good marketing requires us to look beyond output.

Did we solve a real problem?
Did we give people a reason to pay attention?
Did we learn something useful?
Did we make a better decision?

Producing 20 ideas is easy if you have the right tools.

Knowing which idea deserves your time is a different skill.
I don't want to just become faster at doing marketing.
I want to get better at deciding what marketing is worth doing in the first place.

I’m not trying to become better at AI.
I’m trying to become a better marketer who uses AI.

The distinction matters.

Because AI is making execution easier.

I can generate 20 headlines.
10 campaign ideas.
5 positioning angles.
A month of content.

But none of that answers the harder questions:

→ Which idea is actually worth pursuing?
→ What does this audience genuinely care about?
→ What should we say differently?
→ What should we remove?
→ And sometimes, should we do anything at all?

That’s the skill I’m trying to build now.

Not becoming the person who knows the most AI tools.
Becoming the person who can look at 20 possible directions and recognize the one worth pursuing.

I think that’s where marketing is heading.

AI will keep making execution cheaper.

So I want to get better at the things AI can’t decide for me:
What matters.
What resonates.
What’s worth saying.
What’s worth leaving out.

I’m still figuring out what that looks like in practice.
But that’s the marketer I’m trying to become.

The AI gave me 10 options.

My job wasn't to pick the best one.
It was to figure out whether any of them were actually worth using.

I think this is going to become one of the most important skills in marketing.

AI can give you:
→ 10 headlines
→ 20 campaign ideas
→ 5 positioning angles
→ 3 versions of your landing page
→ an entire content calendar

But more options don't automatically mean better marketing.

Sometimes they just give you more mediocre ideas to choose from.

That's why I'm starting to think marketers need to become better editors, not better prompt writers.

Better at asking:
Is this actually relevant to the audience?

Does this solve a real problem?

Is there a reason for someone to care?

Does this sound like us?

What should we remove?

And most importantly:
Is this idea worth pursuing at all?
AI can generate possibilities incredibly fast.
But it doesn't remove the need for judgment.
If anything, it makes judgment more valuable.
Because when everyone can generate more...
The advantage might belong to the person who knows what to leave out.

The more I learn about AI, the less impressed I am by people who know 100 AI tools.

Because knowing the tools is becoming the easy part.
AI can help you:
→ write copy
→ generate ideas
→ analyze data
→ research competitors
→ create visuals
→ build campaigns
So what happens when everyone has access to the same capabilities?

I think the advantage shifts.

From knowing how to execute
to knowing what is worth executing.

From writing a prompt
to asking the right question.

From generating 20 ideas
to recognizing the one idea worth pursuing.

From producing content faster
to knowing what your audience actually cares about.

And honestly, this has changed how I’m thinking about my own journey in marketing.

I don't want to become someone who is simply good at using AI.

I want to become good at thinking like a marketer who knows how to use AI.
Because AI can make mediocre marketing faster.
It can also make a great marketer ridiculously more effective.
The difference isn't the tool.
It's the thinking behind it.
And that's the skill I'm trying to build.

I've written over 50 reels. The ones that flopped almost always died in the first line.
Early on, I thought a flop meant the whole idea was bad. Usually the idea was fine, the first line just gave people no reason to stay.
Here's what actually makes someone stop scrolling:
1. Be specific, fast.
"Some tips for better reels" scrolls past. "The 3-word mistake that kills most reels in the first second" makes you stop. Specific feels true. Vague feels like everyone else.
2. Say one thing.
If your first line teases three ideas, it teases none. One clear promise beats a clever line that means nothing.
3. Open a gap.
Give people a reason to need the next line- a surprising claim, a number that doesn't add up, a "here's what nobody tells you." Curiosity is what keeps a thumb still.
4. Write the hook last.
I write the whole thing, then hunt for the most interesting sentence buried in the middle. That's almost always the real hook. I just didn't start there.
The design, the edit, the music, all of it only matters if the first line earns the second.
What's a hook that stopped your scroll recently? Drop it below, I want to see what's working for people.
